section_summary: This section continues an unidentified study of Philippine society under American rule, moving from caciquism and agrarian inequality through commerce, labor, foreign capital, self-government, public health, religion, law, education, and the arts. It reproduces several examples of modern Filipino poetry and fiction, including a lengthy story about irrigation, poverty, and violence. The final chapter begins an account of Filipino migration to Hawaii and the continental United States, plantation labor, racial hostility, repatriation, and immigration restrictions after the Philippine Independence Act.

subfiles.title: Unidentified study of the Philippines, continuation and Chapters XIII–XVIII
subfiles.about: A wide-ranging study examines Philippine economic, political, social, and cultural development under American rule and begins an account of Filipino emigration to Hawaii and the continental United States.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt opens in the middle of a discussion of caciquism and agrarian reform, then surveys Philippine commerce, foreign ownership, labor, economic dependence on the United States, and the risks attending independence. It assesses Filipino self-government, provincial and municipal administration, health, religion, law, prisons, and mass education. Chapters on cultural life trace indigenous, Spanish, and modern influences and reproduce poetry and fiction by contemporary Filipino writers, including the irrigation tragedy “Water, Water, Water.” The final chapter describes migration to Hawaiian plantations and the American mainland, the experiences of Filipino workers, racial conflict, depression-era repatriation, and immigration restrictions, ending mid-discussion of migrants’ adjustment to American life.
